authoredFrom: Erlang's own reference manual on behaviours and callbacks, and the corpus measurement in script/m60/erlang-construct-probe.ts over 3,939 admitted .erl/.hrl files (otp 36e371a4 + elixir 73b3325, one parse each, no sampling). Two ontology types are RULED here and this fixture is what stops the ruling from being prose. The workstream exists because `overrides` was missing from Bash for a whole wave behind a prose justification while the differential stayed green: the analyzer omitted it, the oracle was written after the ruling, and nothing agrees with nothing. So every construct a probe MEASURED as the nearest thing to the ruled types is written here, and every one of them must produce NO edge. The line numbers are read off the file; the claims are read off Erlang semantics, not off analyzer output — the positive rows below were each checked against what the language says before the analyzer was run.

expectSymbols.name: ontology_no_inheritance
expectSymbols.note: the file names itself; nothing is derived from the filename anywhere in this fixture

expectSymbols.name: own
expectSymbols.note: ER-D30: `-callback own/0` at 48 AND `own/0` at 59 declare ONE identity, so there is ONE symbol and no second member for an edge to point at. `definitionLine` keeps the contract's line without moving the declaration's own.

expectSymbols.name: alt
expectSymbols.note: ONE symbol for two bodies in two `-ifdef`/`-else` branches. `clauseCount: 2` is where the multiplicity lives: exactly one body survives preprocessing, neither replaces the other, and there is no second member to point an edge at.

expectRelationships.note: the MODULE-level fact `-behaviour` states, at the behaviour atom's own line
a published TYPE is a different declaration form from a published function
a `-callback` SIGNATURE names types; this is a dependency of `needed`, not of the module

`-type state() :: {ok, term()} | error.` APPLIES term/0. Erlang type syntax is a DEPENDENCY graph: a bare atom there is an atom LITERAL (`error`), and only an applied name (`term()`) is a type use. This is the nearest thing Erlang has to a supertype clause and it is labelled `references`, never `extends`.
a local call resolving against the file's declared name/arity set
ER-D30: `contains` follows the DEFINITION (59), not the `-callback` contract (48)
the FIRST branch's definition line; the symbol spans both

forbidRelationships.note: RULED, and this fixture carries every construct a corpus probe measured as a candidate. A type-only forbid row is the strongest form of this assertion: NO edge of this label may exist in this file at all, whatever its endpoints.

RULED. Instrument A: the pinned wasm's own table defines 137 named node types (132 distinct), 0 abstract supertype/subtype edges and 52 fields, and NONE of 23 inheritance-shaped node types and none of those 52 fields is in either. Instrument B: 0 inheritance-shaped attributes in 3,939 files.
there is no `#record{}` anywhere in this file — `-type state() :: {ok, term()}` is a tuple, not a record — so the class has nothing to construct

the behaviour-callback supply is REAL and MEASURED (378 `-callback` declarations, 572 `-behaviour` sites, 2,548 identities supplied by exact name AND arity) but it is not an `overrides` edge here: `sample_behaviour`'s callbacks live in another file, and the cross-file channels this repository ships carry bare NAMES, which cannot decide a name/arity identity
a `-callback` merged with its own definition is ONE symbol (ER-D30), so this edge would be `own -> own`: a self-loop carrying no information
two `-ifdef`/`-else` bodies are ALTERNATIVE implementations, not one replacing the other. Exactly one survives preprocessing. The multiplicity is already published as `meta.clauseCount: 2`.
a type APPLYING another type is a dependency (`references`), never a subtype relation. Publishing it as `extends` is the fabricated edge the workstream warns about.
a behaviour is a CONTRACT, not a member: ER-D6 gives it the edge only and never a symbol
a type from another file (or from the type vocabulary) is a reference, not a member of this module
